q: What does an EPSS score of 0.80 mean?
o: An 80% chance the flaw is exploited in the next 30 days
The flaw is 80% as severe as the worst possible flaw
80% of systems running the product are vulnerable
The vendor has fixed 80% of affected versions
why: EPSS, from FIRST, estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days. It measures likelihood, not severity.

q: Which CVSS v3.1 base score range is rated Critical?
o: Only 10.0
why: CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 both rate 9.0-10.0 Critical, 7.0-8.9 High, 4.0-6.9 Medium and 0.1-3.9 Low.

q: What is the CISA KEV catalog?
o: A list of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild
A list of every CVE with a CVSS score of 9 or more
CISA's list of approved security vendors
A database of ransomware decryption keys
why: KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) only lists flaws with evidence of active exploitation and a clear fix or mitigation. US federal agencies must remediate them by a set due date.

q: What is the difference between a CVE and a CWE?
o: A CVE is one specific flaw in a product; a CWE is a category of weakness
A CVE is for software, a CWE is for hardware
A CWE is a CVE that has been exploited
They are two names for the same identifier
why: CVE-2024-3400 is one flaw in one product. CWE-79 (cross-site scripting) is a type of weakness that many CVEs share.

q: What makes a vulnerability a "zero-day"?
o: Attackers exploit it before the vendor has released a fix
It was found on the day the software was released
It can be exploited with zero user interaction
It has a CVSS score of zero
why: Zero-day means defenders have had zero days to patch: exploitation started before a fix existed.

q: In the 3-2-1 backup rule, what does the "1" stand for?
o: One copy kept off-site or offline
One backup per day
One administrator with restore rights
One year of retention
why: Three copies, on two different media, one of them off-site. Many teams now add an immutable or offline copy so ransomware cannot encrypt or delete it.

q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
o: Each account gets only the access it needs to do its job
Administrators get fewer passwords to remember
Users with the fewest privileges are patched last
Privileged accounts are shared to reduce their number
why: Limiting access shrinks what an attacker can reach with any single stolen account.

q: What does TLP:CLEAR mean on a threat report?
o: It can be shared publicly without restriction
It must stay inside your organisation
It may only be shared with named recipients
It has been cleared by legal for court use
why: Traffic Light Protocol 2.0: CLEAR is public, GREEN is for the community, AMBER for the organisation and its clients, RED for named recipients only.

q: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
o: A knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques seen in real attacks
A vulnerability scanner made by MITRE
The US government's list of banned software
A scoring system for vulnerabilities
why: ATT&CK catalogues how attackers behave, from initial access to impact. Teams use it to map detection coverage.

q: Which of these is the strongest protection against MFA phishing?
o: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys
SMS one-time codes
Authenticator app push notifications
Email one-time codes
why: FIDO2 and passkeys are bound to the real website's domain, so a look-alike phishing site cannot capture and replay them. Codes and pushes can be relayed or approved by mistake.

q: What is "MFA fatigue"?
o: Flooding a user with push approval requests until they accept one
Users turning off MFA because it is slow
An MFA server crashing under load
Re-enrolling MFA too often
why: Attackers with a stolen password trigger repeated push prompts, often with a phone call pretending to be IT. Number matching makes this much harder.

q: What is the difference between credential stuffing and password spraying?
o: Stuffing reuses leaked username-password pairs; spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts
Stuffing targets admins; spraying targets users
Spraying uses leaked pairs; stuffing guesses passwords
They are the same attack
why: Stuffing bets on password reuse from other breaches. Spraying stays under lockout limits by trying one or two passwords per account.

q: What is a SIM swap attack?
o: Moving a victim's phone number to an attacker's SIM to receive their calls and SMS codes
Swapping a SIM card to avoid roaming charges
Cloning a SIM card's encryption key over the air
Installing malware through a SIM toolkit app
why: Attackers talk or bribe a mobile carrier into porting the number. SMS-based recovery and MFA codes then go to them.

q: What is business email compromise (BEC)?
o: Fraud using a real or spoofed business mailbox to redirect payments or data
Malware that encrypts email servers
Spam sent from a hacked marketing tool
A denial-of-service attack on mail servers
why: BEC usually needs no malware: a convincing email from a supplier or executive asks for a payment to a new account. Call-back checks on a known number stop most of it.

q: What is "vishing"?
o: Phishing by voice call
Phishing through video ads
Phishing using a virtual machine
Phishing that targets VIPs only
why: Voice phishing, often posing as the help desk, is a common way into SaaS platforms and identity providers.

q: What does an infostealer typically take from an infected computer?
o: Saved passwords, browser session cookies and crypto wallets
Only documents from the desktop
The computer's firmware
Nothing; it only displays adverts
why: Stolen session cookies let attackers skip the password and MFA entirely, which is why infostealer logs fuel so many breaches.

q: What is "OAuth consent phishing"?
o: Tricking a user into granting a malicious app access to their account data
Stealing OAuth server certificates
Guessing OAuth client secrets
Phishing that uses a cookie banner
why: The user never gives away a password: they click Accept, and the attacker's app keeps a token that survives password resets.

q: What is a software supply-chain attack?
o: Compromising a vendor, library or update so the attack reaches the vendor's customers
Stealing laptops in transit
Attacking a company's shipping partner
Buying fake software licences
why: One compromised package or update can reach thousands of organisations at once, as poisoned npm and PyPI releases keep showing.

q: What does Mark of the Web (MotW) do in Windows?
o: Tags downloaded files so Windows warns, opens Office in Protected View and blocks macros
Watermarks files printed from a browser
Blocks access to adult websites
Marks websites as trusted for single sign-on
why: Attackers prize MotW bypass flaws because they remove the warnings that would stop a user opening a malicious download.

q: What is NTLM relay?
o: Forwarding a captured Windows authentication attempt to another server to log in as the victim
Speeding up NTLM logins through a proxy
Cracking NTLM hashes on GPUs
Sending NTLM logs to a SIEM
why: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and Extended Protection for Authentication block relays. Moving off NTLM removes the risk.

q: What does "double extortion" ransomware mean?
o: Encrypting data and also threatening to leak stolen copies
Asking for two ransom payments in a row
Attacking two companies at the same time
Encrypting data twice with two keys
why: Backups do not solve the leak threat, which is why data theft is now the main lever in most ransomware cases.

q: Why do attackers target edge devices such as VPNs and firewalls?
o: They face the internet, hold privileged access and rarely run endpoint security
They are the cheapest devices to buy
They store all of a company's email
They cannot be patched
why: Edge devices dominate CISA's exploited list. They often lack EDR, so intrusions there go unseen for weeks.

q: Which three DNS records protect a domain against email spoofing?
o: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
MX, A and CNAME
TXT, SRV and PTR
DNSSEC, CAA and TLSA
why: SPF lists the senders allowed to mail for the domain, DKIM signs messages, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when both checks fail.

q: What is the main job of EDR software?
o: Detect and respond to suspicious behaviour on endpoints
Encrypt data at rest
Filter spam
Manage user passwords
why: Endpoint Detection and Response records process and network activity on each machine so analysts can spot and contain attacks.

q: Why should a password manager be preferred over reusing one strong password?
o: A breach of one site then exposes only that site's password
It makes passwords shorter
It removes the need for MFA
Websites require it
why: Unique passwords defeat credential stuffing, which relies entirely on reuse.

q: What is a canary token?
o: A fake credential or file that alerts you when someone uses it
A hardware MFA key
A test payment card
A type of TLS certificate
why: No legitimate user should ever touch it, so any use is a high-confidence signal of an intruder.

q: What does "segmentation" mainly limit in an attack?
o: Lateral movement from the first compromised system
The number of phishing emails received
Patch installation time
Licence costs
why: If the network is divided into zones with strict rules between them, one compromised machine cannot reach everything.

q: Which question best decides patch order across a large backlog?
o: Is it exploited (KEV), how likely is exploitation (EPSS), and is the system internet-facing?
Which flaw has the oldest CVE number?
Which vendor released the most patches?
Which patch is the smallest download?
why: CVSS alone rates most flaws High or Critical. Exploitation evidence, likelihood and exposure cut the list to what attackers will actually use.

q: Under DORA, how soon must an EU financial entity send the initial notification of a major ICT incident?
o: Within 4 hours of classifying it as major, and no later than 24 hours after becoming aware of it
Within 72 hours
Within 30 days
Only once the incident is resolved
why: DORA's technical standards set 4 hours from classification (24 hours from detection at most) for the initial report, then the intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial one and the final report within a month after that.

q: Under NIS2, what must an essential or important entity send within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident?
o: An early warning
The final report
A full forensic analysis
A press release
why: NIS2 Article 23: early warning within 24 hours, incident notification within 72 hours, final report within one month.

q: How long does a US-listed company have to file an SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 after deciding a cyber incident is material?
o: Four business days
24 hours
30 days
Until the next quarterly report
why: The SEC's 2023 rules require disclosure within four business days of the materiality determination, with a narrow national-security delay.

q: Under GDPR, how quickly must a controller notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach?
o: Without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware
Within 24 hours
Within 7 business days
Only if more than 1,000 people are affected
why: GDPR Article 33. Notification is not needed when the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms.

q: What does DORA require financial entities to keep about their ICT third-party providers?
o: A register of information on all ICT third-party contractual arrangements
A copy of each provider's source code
Proof that every provider is EU-based
Nothing; DORA only covers internal systems
why: The register feeds supervisors' view of concentration risk, the same risk that shows when one supplier breach hits many banks.

q: What does PCI DSS protect?
o: Payment card data
Personal health records
Government classified information
Source code repositories
why: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard applies to any organisation that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data.

q: What is a CNA in the CVE system?
o: An organisation authorised to assign CVE IDs, often a vendor for its own products
A Cyber Notification Agency run by CISA
A type of exploit kit
A CVSS calculation method
why: CVE Numbering Authorities such as Microsoft, Red Hat or Cisco assign IDs and usually publish their own CVSS score in the CVE record.
